title: Mobile Application Security
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terminology of Mobile Application Security.
Apply mobile application security to a small synthetic example and identify evidence that supports the conclusion.
Identify a relevant limitation or failure mode and describe a safe defensive response.

content.intro: This lesson covers mobile application security in the Mobile, IoT, Wireless, and Operational Technology Security track. It preserves the PDF's listed subtopics and develops a small, checkable defensive example. You will practice stating scope and assumptions, selecting relevant evidence, and describing what remains uncertain.
content.why_it_matters: Consider updateability, physical access, unique identity, supported lifecycle, segmentation, and safe failure modes—especially in OT. The specific focus here is mobile application security; connect each subtopic to an observable check or a documented decision.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Mobile Application Security focuses on mobile threat models; secure local storage; authentication and session handling. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.

items.title: Mobile Threat Models
items.text: AI-enabled applications add risks around untrusted inputs, data exposure, model and dependency provenance, tool permissions, evaluation, and over-trusting generated output. Keep retrieval and tool actions constrained, minimize sensitive data, and use human review for high-impact decisions.

items.title: Secure Local Storage
items.text: For secure local storage, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Authentication and Session Handling
items.text: Authentication verifies a claimed identity; it does not decide all permissions. Use phishing-resistant factors where practical, protect recovery flows, rate-limit failures, and avoid reusing credentials.

items.title: API Communication Security
items.text: API and identity protections must validate protocol details, token issuer/audience/expiry, resource-level permissions, and request limits on the server. Browser CORS policy is not a replacement for authentication or authorization.

items.title: Certificate Validation
items.text: TLS protects a communication channel when peers negotiate an accepted protocol and validate authentication material and names correctly. Certificate handling, renewal, trust stores, and current protocol configuration remain operational responsibilities.

items.title: Application Permissions
items.text: Authorization should be enforced for the exact resource and action on the trusted server. Start with least privilege, deny access by default, and test both allowed and denied paths across roles and tenants.

items.title: Secure Build and Distribution Practices
items.text: For secure build and distribution practices, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Mobile Security Testing Standards
items.text: Governance defines accountability and connects requirements to controls, evidence, exceptions, and review cadence. Framework mappings are aids to coverage, not proof of compliance or a substitute for legal interpretation.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification
content_blocks.text: Mobile, IoT, wireless, and operational technology systems have platform and safety constraints that change how controls are deployed. Before attempting any live security test, obtain explicit permission and verify that the target and method are within scope. When a secure isolated runner is not available, treat the code as a local/synthetic example and do not run arbitrary content on production infrastructure.

content_blocks.title: Run, verify, and reset
content_blocks.text: Review the python snippet as a local calculation. If you choose to run this example, use Python 3 and synthetic inputs in a disposable local environment; compare the displayed expected output with what you observe. If the result differs, check the copied inputs and runtime version, restore the synthetic input, and repeat. No scan, external request, or production change is needed.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Mobile Application Security focuses on mobile threat models; secure local storage; authentication and session handling. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case. Apply this to one controlled example, record evidence, and note an important edge case. Next, continue to the next lesson or revisit the prerequisite concept if a key term is unclear.

content.task: Create a concise, reviewable artifact demonstrating Mobile Application Security. Use synthetic data or a controlled local training environment only. Include the relevant syllabus subtopics (Mobile Threat Models; Secure Local Storage; Authentication and Session Handling), state assumptions, show what evidence would support your conclusion, identify one failure mode, and recommend a defensive next step. Do not test systems outside written authorization.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use only a synthetic dataset, a disposable local lab, or an explicitly authorized system.
Include a clear scope/assumption statement and enough sanitized evidence for another learner to follow the reasoning.
Explain one limitation, edge case, or failure mode.
Recommend a proportionate defensive control and describe how to verify it safely.
hints: Write the expected behavior and test boundary before looking at a result.
Change one assumption at a time; compare results against the original synthetic case.
Record evidence and uncertainty separately, and select a proportionate protective action.
content.expected_output:
asset: iot-demo-01
review: plan replacement or isolation
review: verify required access only
troubleshooting: The example is illustrative and should be reviewed against current platform/version documentation before production use.
If an output differs, check the input and runtime version; do not broaden the activity to an unrelated system.
Use only fake data and remove all temporary local artifacts when the exercise is complete.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one observation as conclusive proof.
common_mistakes.why: Security telemetry and tests cover only the cases they were designed to observe.
common_mistakes.fix: Corroborate important claims and document coverage gaps.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing a target without confirming authorization.
common_mistakes.why: A technical ability to reach a system does not grant permission to assess it.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic input or a local lab; stop if the approved scope is unclear.

common_mistakes.problem: Skipping the version and context assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Security controls and protocol details vary across implementations and deployment models.
common_mistakes.fix: Record versions, configuration, expected output, and the source used for verification.

summary: Mobile Application Security is best understood within its defined scope and trust boundaries.
Use relevant evidence and test both an expected case and a meaningful failure case.
Record uncertainty and choose a proportionate, authorized defensive next step.

sources.notes: CSF 2.0 defines outcome-oriented functions and does not prescribe one mandatory implementation. Verify the current CSF resources before publication.

sources.notes: CIS v8.1 aligns control mappings with NIST CSF 2.0. Select safeguards according to context, risk, and operating constraints.
